headline_case: Sentence case dominates for titles and H2s (e.g. "Comprehensive guide to skill testing: all you need to understand", "What are the characteristics of Generation X?"); glossary page titles use Title Case for the term itself ("Blue-Collar Worker", "Appointment Schedule"); numbered H3 subheads are sometimes fully lowercase ("### 1. financial management")
quote_style: curly (curly double quotes for scare quotes like “bridge” and cited phrases; curly single quotes also frequent for terms like ‘forgotten generation’, ‘no-poach’); straight quotes essentially absent
industry_terms: skill tests / skills tests (both forms appear)
mixed US/UK spelling: mostly US (organizations, labor) but UK forms appear in some glossary entries (labour, misdemeanour, organising, recognise)
use-it-or-lose-it (hyphenated as modifier, also styled “use it or lose it” in quotes)
full-time / part-time (hyphenated as modifiers, but “full time” appears unhyphenated in the FTE title)
labor (US spelling in most posts) vs labour (UK spelling throughout the Labour Force Participation Rate post — inconsistent across the set)
skills assessment / skills-based hiring (hyphenated as modifier)
non-exempt vs exempt (mostly hyphenated 'non-exempt', but 'nonexempt' appears once)
pink collar / white collar / blue collar (inconsistent: open compound as noun, sometimes hyphenated as modifier — 'pink-collar roles' and 'pink collar jobs' both appear)
situational judgment (US spelling dominates; one 'judgement' slip)
preferred_words: attract and retain top talent (recurring boilerplate phrase)
employees (never “staff” or “workers” in HR context; “workers” reserved for safety/labor-law posts)
benefit (singular, as in “a benefit for both employer and employee”)
typically / commonly (as hedges instead of “usually” alone)
candidates (not applicants, except in volume-screening context)
recruiters / TA teams / hiring managers (the reader is addressed as the hirer)
employees (Walmart context switches to 'associates', matching the brand)
organization / organizational (US -ize/-or spellings throughout: customize, standardize, labor; one 'labour'/'behaviours'/'specialised' slip in newer entries)
skills (plural, as in 'skills test', 'skills assessment' — never 'skill test')
ensure (the workhorse verb for compliance claims)
structured (structured hiring plan, structured interviews, structured assessment)
avoided_words: “attract and retain top talent” — a boilerplate closing sentence pasted near-verbatim into at least four posts ("helping organizations attract and retain top talent")
“It’s important to note that…” (appears in multiple posts)
“Let’s take a few real-life scenarios” (chatty filler)
dangling citation fragments pasted mid-sentence with no content (“HBR’s labor economics research”, “SHRM’s workforce planning guidance” left hanging as incomplete sentences)
delve ("we will delve into the essence of binary code")
cornerstone / backbone / underpins (stacked in the Binary code intro)
drives improvement / drives results (boilerplate CTA sentence pasted verbatim into multiple glossary entries)
brand_naming: batch1: Testlify written as one word with capital T; product features referred to generically in lowercase ("pre-employment assessments", "skills tests", "hiring plan") rather than as capitalized product names; third-party brands capitalized per owner (SAP, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics, Workday, UKG); generational cohorts capitalized (Generation X, Gen X, Millennials, Baby Boomers); acronym-styled terms keep internal caps (O*NET/O*Net used inconsistently, ERP, CRM, ESS) | batch2: The company name "Testlify" never appears in body copy of these posts (only in URLs); the brand is referenced obliquely via generic product phrases in lowercase: "skills assessment", "pre-employment assessments", "talent acquisition", "hiring plan". No named products are capitalized or mentioned. | batch3: Testlify — always one word, capital T only, never all-caps or hyphenated; possessive used freely ("Testlify's pre-employment assessments"). Other brands written in their own house style (Walmart, McDonald's Hamburger University, Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, LinkedIn). Products/features stay lowercase ("skills assessment platform", "cognitive ability tests")
em_dash_usage: batch1: True em dashes are rare; parenthetical breaks use a spaced hyphen/en dash (" – ") as in "manual labour or skilled trades – typically in manufacturing"; a spaced colon (" : ") appears repeatedly where a dash would normally go ("most overlooked generation in talent strategy : despite holding..."); hyphens used for ranges (1965-1980, $80,000-$120,000, 14-day) and compound modifiers (data-driven, skills-based, do-not-hire) | batch2: True em dashes are rare; asides are set with a spaced en dash/hyphen (" – "): "the right people – with the right skills – are available", "a portable, industry-recognized credential". Several posts also contain a spaced colon (" : ") where a dash clearly belongs ("temporary coverage : aligning", "the talent pool contracts : creating"), an apparent conversion artifact. Hyphens are used for numeric ranges (15-20%, 1-6 years, 100-300+) and compound modifiers (pre-tax, mobile-first, cause-based). | batch3: Hyphens do the heavy lifting: numeric ranges are always hyphenated with no spaces (2-3 weeks, 60-90 minutes, $16-17 million, 30-40%). Spaced em dashes ( — ) appear only in the newer glossary entries (White Collar Worker) for asides and definitions; the Seasonal entry uses spaced en dashes/hyphens ( – ) the same way. Several glossary entries have a stray spaced colon ( : ) where a dash belongs ("An EIN : also called a FEIN : is..."), an artifact worth noting
ellipses: batch1: Essentially never used; the only "etc." style trailing appears in parenthetical lists ("active listening, etc."); no rhetorical ellipses observed | batch2: Essentially absent — no ellipses observed in any of the nine posts except mid-sentence truncation from page cutoffs; not a stylistic device used by the writers. | batch3: Essentially never used — zero true ellipses across all eight posts; open-ended lists end with "etc." or "and so on" instead
number_style: batch1: Numerals dominate throughout: percentages as numeral+% (76%, 20-30%, 5-8%), currency as $+numeral ($7.25/hour, $20-100, $80,000-$120,000+), multipliers as 1.5x, years and ranges numeric (1965-1980, 14-day notice, 40 in a workweek); small numbers occasionally spelled out in running prose ("six reasons", "two dozen states"); list items numbered with digits | batch2: Numerals dominate everywhere, including small numbers ("3 to 6-month break", "after 5 years", "6 core components", "7:10 years" [typo for 7-10]); % symbol with numerals (80%, 15-20%, 7.65%, 50%); $ symbol with numerals ($7.25 per hour, $3,200, $610, Rs 1,500); hyphenated ranges (3-5%, 25-54, 2014 and 2018); measurements as "40 hours/week" or "40-hour workweek"; dates as "January 31" and "January 31st" (inconsistent); occasional spelled-out numbers slip in ("between one and six months", "two steps"). | batch3: Numerals dominate, even below 10 ("3-5 days", "one or two brief rounds" is the rare spelled-out case). Percentages always numeral+% with no space (45%, 56%, 60-70%). Currency as $+numeral ($20 per hour, $684/week, $16-17 million). Large counts use commas (500,000) or K shorthand (500K+, $500K-$2M). Multipliers as digit+x (1.5x, 200-300x). Ranges hyphenated without spaces. Times/durations in numerals (30 mins, 60-90 mins)
